Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes. I have full content from **enduringword.com** (Pentecostal/charismatic), **preceptaustin.org** (evangelical), **Gill's Exposition** (older Baptist, via biblehub.com), and **monergism.com** (hosting Martin Luther's commentary — Reformed/Lutheran). I also have substantial search excerpts from Ligonier (Reformed), Desiring God (Baptist), Spurgeon, and others.

---

# 1 Corinthians 13 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## The Context

The chapter sits between Paul's teaching on spiritual gifts (ch. 12) and his regulations for their orderly use (ch. 14). The Corinthians were enamoured with "showy" gifts like tongues and prophecy, using them pridefully and divisively. Paul insists that love (*agape*)—not giftedness—is the true measure of spiritual maturity.

- **Enduring Word**: "Paul cuts through the Corinthians' fascination with flashy gifts...to declare that without love, all of it amounts to nothing." [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **Precept Austin**: "The Corinthians were impatient with each other, suing each other, tolerating sin in the church, and creating problems because they did not have love." [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-13-commentary)
- **Monergism (Luther)**: "Paul's purpose in this chapter is to silence and humble haughty Christians, particularly teachers and preachers...Each seeks his own honor and advantage, desiring to gain preferment and precedence over others." [monergism.com](https://www.monergism.com/pauls-praise-christian-love-1-corinthians-13)

---

## v. 1: *"If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am only a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal."*

**Traditional Reading (all traditions agree on the main point):**

- Paul begins with the gift most prized at Corinth—tongues. Even if one could speak every human language and even the language of angels, without love the speech is mere noise. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **Gill**: The "tongues of men" means all human languages (the Jews counted 70 languages at Babel). The "tongues of angels" may refer to the most excellent, eloquent speech imaginable. Love is the indispensable grace. [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/13.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/13.htm)
- **Precept Austin**: The five "ifs" in vv. 1–3 are all third-class conditional sentences — they describe potential (hypothetical) actions. Paul is not saying it is possible for men to speak angelic languages; he is making a rhetorical point. [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-13-commentary)
- "Ringing gong or clanging cymbal": These were used in pagan worship in Corinth; the image is of an empty, chaotic noise — loud but meaningless. [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-13-commentary)

**Denominational Differences:**

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)**: Takes "tongues of angels" more literally — "there are angelic languages men can speak by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit." The genuine gift of tongues may not be a living human language but a supernatural heavenly language. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **Reformed/Lutheran (Luther via Monergism)**: Insists "tongues of angels" is a deliberately impossible hypothetical. "There is no angelic tongue; while angels may speak to us in a human tongue men can never speak in those of angels." Paul uses hyperbole for emphasis. [monergism.com](https://www.monergism.com/pauls-praise-christian-love-1-corinthians-13)
- **Reformed (Ligonier / R.C. Sproul)**: "Though we believe speaking in tongues and the gift of prophecy ceased with the end of the apostolic age, the many spiritual gifts...can still be used in an unloving manner." [learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/priority-love](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/priority-love)

---

## v. 2: *"If I have the gift of prophecy and can fathom all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have absolute faith so as to move mountains, but have not love, I am nothing."*

**Traditional Reading:**

- Paul escalates: prophecy, all mysteries, all knowledge, mountain-moving faith — these are the most impressive spiritual endowments imaginable, yet without love the person possessing them is "nothing" (Greek *oudeis* — absolutely nothing, not merely relatively nothing). [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-13-commentary)
- **Gill**: "All faith" here is not saving faith (which cannot exist without love) but the faith of miracles — the supernatural ability to perform wonders. A person may have this and yet lack regenerating grace. [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/13.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/13.htm)
- **Luther (Monergism)**: "Mountain-moving faith" is an impossible hypothetical, just like "tongues of angels." Paul's point is that love is so essential that even the greatest conceivable faith would be nothing without it. Three interpretations are possible: (1) Paul means a general (non-saving) faith in God's power, which Judas had; (2) true believers may fall from faith through pride; or (3) — Luther's preferred — Paul is making an "impossible supposition" for rhetorical force. [monergism.com](https://www.monergism.com/pauls-praise-christian-love-1-corinthians-13)
- "Remove mountains" alludes to Jesus' words in Matthew 17:20. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)

---

## v. 3: *"If I give all I possess to the poor and exult in the surrender of my body, but have not love, I gain nothing."*

**Traditional Reading:**

- Even total self-sacrifice — giving away all possessions (what Jesus told the rich young ruler to do) and surrendering one's body in martyrdom — profits nothing without love as the motive. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **Gill**: The Jews had examples of men who gave away all goods to the poor, but did so for honour and to merit eternal life, not from love. Similarly, some sought martyrdom for fame. [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/13.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/13.htm)
- **Luther**: "Were I to perform all the good works on earth and yet had not charity—having sought therein only my own honor and profit and not my neighbor's—I would nevertheless be lost." The key is the motive. [monergism.com](https://www.monergism.com/pauls-praise-christian-love-1-corinthians-13)

**Textual Variant (well-known):**

- The BSB reads "exult in the surrender of my body" (or "give my body to be burned"). Some ancient manuscripts read "give my body that I may glory" (or "that I may boast"). The difference is minor, but the variant reading sharpens the point: even martyrdom sought for personal glory is worthless.
- **Peake's Commentary** (modern scholarship, via studylight.org): Notes the uncertainty: "RVm, 'that I may glory,' is very strongly attested, and accepted by WH and Harnack...If the object of the surrender is that he may boast, the love of glory empties the act." Also notes the "burning" is probably not execution but self-immolation — citing the example of an Indian gymnosophist who burned himself alive in the time of Alexander the Great, whose tomb Paul may have seen in Athens. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/1-corinthians-13.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/1-corinthians-13.html)
- **Enduring Word**: Acknowledges the textual variant but says "the meaning is the same, and the difference is really minor." [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)

---

## v. 4a: *"Love is patient, love is kind."*

**Traditional Reading:**

- Paul now describes love through action-verbs, not abstract concepts. True love is always demonstrated in behaviour. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **"Patient" (longsuffering)**: The Greek *makrothumei* — used of the person who is wronged and has power to avenge but chooses mercy. It reflects God's own character (2 Peter 3:9). [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **"Kind"**: Simple, practical goodness. Gill: "Liberal and bountiful, does good to all men, even to enemies." [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/13.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/13.htm)
- **Luther**: "Love suffereth long" means it is not hasty to exercise revenge. "Love is kind" means pleasant to deal with, kind to all in words, acts and attitude. [monergism.com](https://www.monergism.com/pauls-praise-christian-love-1-corinthians-13)
- **Precept Austin**: Both verbs are in the present tense — love *continually* suffers long and *continually* is kind. [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-13-commentary)

---

## vv. 4b–6: *"It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. It is not rude, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no account of wrongs. Love takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth."*

**Traditional Reading (all agree):**

- **"Does not envy"**: Envy is uniquely destructive. It murdered Abel, enslaved Joseph, and put Jesus on the cross (Matthew 27:18). [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **"Does not boast / is not puffed up"**: Both relate to pride — "love doesn't get its head swelled." Spiritual pride is the worst kind. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **"Is not rude"**: Love displays good manners and kindness in behaviour. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **"Not self-seeking"**: Love is others-centred, not self-centred (cf. Philippians 2:4, Romans 12:10). [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **"Not easily angered"**: Love does not have a short fuse. Moses lost the Promised Land because he became provoked (Numbers 20:2–11). [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **"Keeps no account of wrongs"**: Literally "does not store up the memory of any wrong." Love does not maintain a ledger of grievances. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **"Takes no pleasure in evil but rejoices in the truth"**: Love is never glad when wrongdoing prevails; it celebrates truth and righteousness.

**Luther's distinctive reading of "rejoices not in iniquity"**: He takes this as referring to *malicious rejoicing at another's sin and fall*. False teachers prefer to hear that someone else has done wrong and been brought to shame, so they themselves appear more righteous. Love is the opposite — it grieves at another's wrong and rejoices at another's right-doing. [monergism.com](https://www.monergism.com/pauls-praise-christian-love-1-corinthians-13)

**Baptist (Desiring God / John Piper — via search excerpt)**: Notes that 13 of the 15 elements in vv. 4–7 fall into two main categories: (1) love is durable and doesn't give up, and (2) love is not proud. "Is it not surprising that the opposite of love in 1 Corinthians 13 is not hate but pride." [desiringgod.org/articles/what-love-does-and-does-not-do](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/what-love-does-and-does-not-do)

---

## v. 7: *"It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things."*

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Spurgeon** called these "love's four sweet companions." [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **"Bears all things"**: The Greek can also mean "covers" — i.e., love covers a multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8). Spurgeon: "Love stands in the presence of a fault, with a finger on her lip." [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **"Believes all things"**: Not gullibility, but a disposition to believe the best about others unless facts demand otherwise. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **"Hopes all things"**: Love is fundamentally optimistic, not pessimistic. Even when hurt, it hopes for better.
- **"Endures all things"**: The greatness of agape is that it *keeps on* bearing, believing, and hoping. It doesn't give up. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **Spurgeon**: "If your brethren are angry without a cause, be sorry for them, but do not let them conquer you by driving you into a bad temper. Stand fast in love; endure not some things, but all things, for Christ's sake." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/1-corinthians-13.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/1-corinthians-13.html) (from search excerpt)
- **Luther**: "'Beareth all things' — it excuses every failing in all men." "'Believeth all things' — love is of decidedly trustful disposition...He measures all other hearts by his own." "'Hopeth all things' — love despairs of no man, however wicked." "'Endureth all things' — it continues to do good everywhere, notwithstanding its services must be rewarded by evil." [monergism.com](https://www.monergism.com/pauls-praise-christian-love-1-corinthians-13)

---

## v. 8: *"Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will cease; where there are tongues, they will be restrained; where there is knowledge, it will be dismissed."*

**Traditional Reading (all agree on the core point):**

- Love is permanent; the spiritual gifts are temporary. This is Paul's central contrast. The gifts are "temporary containers" of God's work; love is the work itself. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **Gill**: "The gifts of knowledge, speaking with tongues, and preaching, shall fail, but this [love] will not." [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/13.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/13.htm)

**The Cessationist/Continuationist Debate (major Protestant difference):**

This verse and v. 10 ("when the perfect comes") are the key battleground between those who believe the miraculous gifts ceased with the apostolic age (cessationists) and those who believe they continue today (continuationists).

- **Cessationist (Reformed / Ligonier / R.C. Sproul)**: "We believe speaking in tongues and the gift of prophecy ceased with the end of the apostolic age." [learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/priority-love](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/priority-love)
- **Cessationist (Baptist / Garner-Howes)**: Argues that "tongues...shall cease" means they stopped when the Bible was completed. On v. 13: "some [gifts] were given...for a limited time only, until the Bible was completed — thereafter only three gifts remained [faith, hope, love]." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-corinthians-13.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-corinthians-13.html)
- **Continuationist (Pentecostal / Enduring Word / David Guzik)**: "Virtually all commentators agree 'that which is perfect' is fulfilled when we are in the eternal presence of the Perfect One...Though some that believe the miraculous gifts ceased with the apostles say it refers to the completion of the New Testament, they are wrong." Also notes that the argument about the middle voice of "will cease" (i.e., tongues will stop *by themselves*) is "disregarded by virtually all scholars of ancient Greek." [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **Reformed (Calvin — cited by Enduring Word)**: "But when will that perfection come? It begins, indeed, at death, because then we put off many weaknesses along with the body." Calvin saw "the perfect" as the eternal state. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **Luther**: The gifts "are bestowed only for this present life, to serve in the administering of the ministerial office. Prophecy, tongues, knowledge, all must cease; for in yonder life each individual will himself perceive perfectly and there will be no need for one to teach another." [monergism.com](https://www.monergism.com/pauls-praise-christian-love-1-corinthians-13)

---

## vv. 9–10: *"For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial passes away."*

**The Identity of "the Perfect" (*to teleion*):**

- **Eternal state / Christ's return**: Enduring Word argues that *telos* in the NT consistently points to the coming of Jesus (1 Cor 1:8, 15:24, James 5:11, Revelation 20:5, 20:7, 21:6, 22:13). "That which is perfect" is when believers are in the eternal presence of God. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **Luther**: "When that which is perfect is come" refers to the life of divine vision in heaven, where faith gives way to sight, and preaching/prophecy/tongues are no longer needed. [monergism.com](https://www.monergism.com/pauls-praise-christian-love-1-corinthians-13)
- **Gill**: The imperfect gifts "must be removed in a perfect state of things" — i.e., the eternal state. [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/13.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/13.htm)
- **Cessationist alternative**: Some (e.g., MacArthur, Garner-Howes Baptist) argue "the perfect" is the completed canon of Scripture. This is a minority view but held in some conservative Baptist and Reformed circles.

---

## v. 11: *"When I was a child, I talked like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I set aside childish ways."*

**Traditional Reading:**

- Paul uses the child-to-man illustration to show that the gifts belong to the present, immature stage of God's people. They are "childish" only in the sense of being appropriate to this age but not to the age to come — not that they are foolish. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **Luther**: "To children, who are yet weak, play is a necessity; it is a substitute for office and work. Similarly, we in the present life are far too frail to behold God. Until we are able, it is necessary that we should use the medium of Word and faith, which are adapted to our limitations." [monergism.com](https://www.monergism.com/pauls-praise-christian-love-1-corinthians-13)
- **Gill**: The present imperfect state is compared to childhood; the future perfect state to manhood. [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/13.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/13.htm)

---

## v. 12: *"Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known."*

**Traditional Reading:**

- Ancient mirrors were polished metal, giving only an indistinct, dim reflection — not the clear glass mirrors of today. Our present knowledge of God is indirect and imperfect; in the eternal state it will be direct and complete. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **"Face to face"**: Paul uses this phrase to describe complete, unhindered fellowship with God (cf. Numbers 12:8, 1 John 3:2). [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **Luther**: "Faith is an imperfect, obscure vision...But the mode of possessing God in the future life is not faith but sight. This is perfect knowledge, rendering unnecessary the Word, and likewise preaching, tongues and prophecy." [monergism.com](https://www.monergism.com/pauls-praise-christian-love-1-corinthians-13)
- **Gill**: The present imperfect knowledge is like looking at objects through a glass or an enigma/riddle; the future perfect knowledge is "face to face, without any artificial help." [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/13.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/13.htm)
- **Peake's Commentary**: "All our apprehension of spiritual realities is at present indirect and indistinct, such as is gained from the reflection in a metal mirror; then it will be direct, immediate, clear, vision face to face (Numbers 12:8)." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/1-corinthians-13.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/1-corinthians-13.html)

---

## v. 13: *"And now these three remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love."*

**Traditional Reading (all traditions agree on the core point):**

- Faith, hope, and love are the three great abiding virtues. Gifts come and go; these three remain. But love is the greatest. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **Why is love greatest?** (1) It will continue, even grow, in the eternal state. Faith becomes sight; hope becomes possession; but love never ends. (2) Love is the very nature of God (1 John 4:8). (3) Love is the fulfilling of the law (Romans 13:10). [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-13/)
- **Gill**: Love is greatest "because of its duration and use." Faith and hope are for oneself; love serves others. "In the other world, faith will be changed for vision, and hope for enjoyment, but love will abide, and be in its full perfection and constant exercise, to all eternity." [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/13.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/13.htm)
- **Luther**: Love "abides forever, also in the life to come. It never gives up, never permits itself to be hindered or defeated by the wickedness or ingratitude of men." [monergism.com](https://www.monergism.com/pauls-praise-christian-love-1-corinthians-13)

**Baptist (Garner-Howes — distinctive view):** Argues that "these three" are the three permanent *spiritual gifts* that remain in the church (faith, hope, love — all charismatic gifts), not merely virtues. "Thereafter only three gifts remained; any person who can count to or spell 'three' should understand." This ties into the cessationist argument that the miraculous gifts ended when Scripture was completed. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-corinthians-13.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-corinthians-13.html)

---

| | The completed canon of Scripture | Some Reformed/Baptist cessationists (MacArthur, Garner-Howes) | [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-corinthians-13.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-corinthians-13.html) |
